claims.text: Premelting and melting behavior of HEA nanoparticles is governed primarily by temperature-induced surface segregation of lower-melting-point elements.
Surface segregation of lower-melting-point elements reduces nanoparticle surface free energy.
The segregated surface initiates localized softening before complete nanoparticle melting.
Arc melting followed by rapid quenching or gas-phase synthesis can produce HEA nanoparticles with homogeneous bulk composition and initially well-mixed surfaces.
A suitable surface passivation treatment can inhibit elemental surface segregation during thermal ramping.
Vacuum or inert atmospheres avoid oxidation during the heating experiment.
Surface effects dominate the thermal behavior of HEA nanoparticles approximately 5–50 nm in size.
Heating produces a chemically heterogeneous nanoparticle skin enriched in low-melting-point elements.
Enrichment of low-melting-point elements at the surface lowers local cohesive energy.
As temperature increases, elements with lower intrinsic melting points preferentially diffuse toward the nanoparticle surface.
Preferential migration of lower-melting-point elements to the surface minimizes the alloy nanoparticle's overall free energy.
The segregated surface layer has a lower effective melting temperature than the nanoparticle bulk.
Inhibiting surface segregation through passivation delays or diminishes the onset of premelting.
Untreated HEA nanoparticles exhibit surface softening or a quasi-liquid surface layer below the bulk melting point.
Passivated nanoparticles retain a higher effective surface-melting temperature than otherwise identical untreated nanoparticles.
The proposed mechanism applies to alloys whose constituent melting points differ by at least approximately 150 °C.
Nanoparticle curvature and local composition gradients can modulate segregation and premelting behavior.
